title: Halvorsen & Sons
text:
The appointment was 09:00, on the record.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked to <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> and took the stairs at <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen Civic Recovery</entity> two at a time. The firm still listed itself in the directory in that careful serif font that said *we have been here longer than you have* — third floor of a corner block, the kind of place where the filing system predated cloud storage and nobody had bothered to argue about it. On the second-floor landing he had the work terminal out before he'd decided to reach for it — habit. The way you check for a pulse on something that might already be dead.

He expected it to have something to say. A meeting at the firm behind the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity> job should have pulled a scope update out of the client, or a query, or at least the dry territorial note it had sent the morning he first walked into <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s shop. It had opinions about where he took its business.

The screen was blank.

Not locked. Not sleeping. Not stalled, not loading. Blank the way a room is blank after someone has quietly stood up and left it — the kind of blank that meant the device had stopped talking to whatever it had been talking to for eleven years. He held it, waiting for the flicker of a boot sequence, the return of the standing contract, the amendment that had started as logistics and become something else entirely.

Nothing came back.

He read the empty screen twice. 08:58. He put the terminal away and went up.

The office had two desks. Blue Hat — her professional name was apparently beside the point for both of them — sat at the nearer one with all her attention aimed at anything except <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. It was costing her something.

Her boss was a big man going gray at the temples, both hands flat on the desk before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat down. It was the posture of a man holding himself back — not a threat. Something closer to embarrassment doing its best to pass as composure. He had an <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a4-71f6-b46a-94ef8cb2348f">Arcturus</entity> cert on the wall, forty years of work behind the name on the glass, and red at the corners of his eyes. Not today's red. The kind that builds up over years.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity>," he said. "Walt. Operations foreman." He shook hands without theater. "The <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity> run."

"Mach six," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Mach six," <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> agreed, with the tiredness of a man who has said those two words in front of lawyers. "My father started this company. Forty-one years ago, him and a partner. Never a finding. Never a suspension. Not one." He pulled a breath that didn't quite settle. "The insurance carrier sent their first letter eight days after <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity>. Their second ran nine pages. I've been on the line with our council rep three times, explaining why a fish-box truck was hauling <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> work product the night your tag went to the Netherlands." He looked at the desk a long moment. "We were used. Somebody walked a fake job through my intake process, and we didn't catch it, because we were good and trusted and didn't ask the question you always have to ask."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the cert on the wall instead of at <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity>'s face. Forty-one years. His own client had opened its screen nine days back and said nothing at all — the first silence in eleven years — and here was a man who'd built something clean for four decades watching it come apart from the inside because somebody needed a name to hide behind. He filed the coincidence and didn't reach for it.

"You're asking it now," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"I'm asking it now." <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> lifted a folder. "My intake desk found the sloppiness first. A client-reference header that carried through from their own internal system. An export error — the kind that happens when someone forgets to clean the metadata before sending a file to a firm they mean to use once and throw away." He set the folder down. "Two words on the header line."

He waited.

"<entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity>."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let the words sit. The building carried someone else's morning up the stairwell, boiler heat and old paper. It was a tidy operation up here — a board of open jobs behind <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity>, each one numbered instead of named. Forty-one years of not getting sloppy, and then sloppy once, from the outside, in a way that would never show up as theirs on any ledger but the one that mattered to them.

"I'll deal with that separately," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. It came out flatter than he meant it. <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> didn't need to know he was already carrying two other threads with the same two words woven through them, or that he had no idea yet how many hands they touched.

"One job. One clean credited recovery, on the public record. Something a court reads and files under routine." <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> produced a second folder, thicker, sealed. "A clinic in West Town — <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> Free Medical. Grant-funded, run on goodwill. Kessler and Sons in the South Loop impounded their med-printer. Kessler works with a distress-paper broker named Arpad Fekete. Fekete scouts clinics behind on their lease maintenance, buys the paper before the grace period closes, and tips Kessler the window."

"The lapse on the clinic."

"Fourteen days. The grace period is ten. The paper sold to Fekete's broker on day nine — inside the window, before it closed." His mouth was flat. "The printer's a Lenz-Haas RP-7. The clinic financed it at Φ640 through the Territory Health Co-Op. Two payments left, and nothing to make them with, because the printer's sitting in bay three of Kessler's yard." He pushed the folder over. "I've had the chain documented for a month. I can't move on it alone. Kessler's yard is family-staffed, and the family has a cousin on the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> council."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> opened the folder. Financing certificate. Maintenance log. The distress-paper sale, timestamped day nine — a single day inside the window. A photograph of the RP-7 in institutional white, the clinic's intake number taped to the chassis, hand-labeled, the tape cut with scissors instead of torn. The kind of label that comes from a place doing its best. Below it, the Co-Op's own repayment card, the boxes filled in by hand and initialed each month — the sort of clinic that still kept a paper ledger because half its patients didn't carry terminals and the other half didn't trust the ones that did.

He thought of the Glove's survey — engineer-grade, correct in every particular except the one that mattered — and set the thought down before it could turn into a speech. <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> didn't need the comparison. He needed the printer back.

"Standard rate," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "And I keep a copy of your engagement file."

<entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> reached into the same drawer and set a second folder on the desk, already prepared.

"Had two copies made," he said. "Yours is on top."

The logistics took the rest of the morning.

A writ at the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> filing desk: Φ40, forty minutes, a clerk who triple-dated every document on principle and brought the stamp down like accuracy was a physical discipline. A truck from <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity>'s pool: Φ25, four hours, matched to Kessler's yard specs so nothing would flag at the gate.

He messaged <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> a time and a place. She was already on the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> apron when he arrived at noon, reading the clinic's posted hours like a woman memorizing a load spec.

Six feet of canvas work jacket, pockets reinforced twice over. Her eyes crossed the front of the building and came back to the angle of the apron, already working out how the printer would ride. She spent forty words a day and wouldn't waste one indoors.

"Bay three," she said. Seven down, thirty-three to go.

"Bay three," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> confirmed.

At the clinic door, a nurse in green scrubs was talking a patient down over the threshold. Both of them wore the look of people used to checking the apron for something that should have been there and wasn't.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> read the sign — NO FEE FOR CARE, hand-painted, black on white, the letters thinning where the brush ran low. She looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>.

"Good printer?" she asked.

"Financed clean. Two payments left."

She nodded once, like that settled something, and went to check the rigging. She coiled the crane cable first, each loop exact, no slack, no kinks — the same care she'd have given a wound.

The truck was where <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had left it. A yard coordinator from the neighboring depot had planted himself behind the rear gate, clipboard out, young, pressed uniform, the kind of posture that came from a training manual instead of years on a dock.

"Who authorized a four-hour hold on a Kessler-spec vehicle without a counter-signature from Kessler's logistics chain?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulled the writ and held it out flat, letting the man take his time.

The coordinator read it. Read it again. Checked the seal against a reference card from his own pocket. Found nothing actionable and went looking anyway — turned the page over, checked the back for a signature that wasn't required, held it up to the light like the paper itself might confess something the words hadn't.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched him do it. Recognized the shape of it: a man who'd been told competence meant never letting a thing through, and had built a whole morning's worth of authority on top of that instruction, and couldn't tell the difference anymore between diligence and stalling. Bay three was thirty minutes out. Every minute this cost was a minute <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> didn't have to spend somewhere else, a minute the clinic's printer sat further behind on its own clock.

He didn't raise his voice. He didn't repeat himself. He stood with the writ still out, arm level, and waited the way he'd waited on a dock ramp for a countdown to hit one second — patient because patience was the only lever that worked, and because the paperwork existed for exactly this, a wall he could put between himself and a fight that wouldn't get the printer to bay three any faster.

The coordinator found a third thing to question — the truck's registration date, two years old, nothing to do with anything — and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> handed him that answer too, and watched him run out of things to ask before he ran out of wanting to ask them. His jaw worked once, then settled.

Forty minutes gone. The gate came down. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> was already moving before it finished rising, the rigging in her hands like she'd been holding the shape of it in her head the whole time she stood there reading a sign about free care.

Kessler and Sons took up a quarter-block on the South Loop fringe: cracked concrete apron, chain-link fence rusting at the joints, three cameras someone had aimed at the street instead of the lot — installed for the look of liability coverage, not the fact of it. The gate was the old kind: a clip-framed window, a hand-lettered sign, a yard dog chained behind the shed that had given up barking at strangers and now just watched.

The old man behind the window had the face of someone who'd sat in that chair thirty years and watched better paper than this come through. He read the writ. Read it again. Found the line he wanted: RECOVERY AGENT OF RECORD: <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">HALVORSEN CIVIC RECOVERY</entity> LLC, BUCKTOWN.

"Arpad's paper," he said.

"Sold inside the grace window," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Timestamps are on page two. The co-op filing desk is open until seventeen hundred if the yard wants to contest it."

The yard manager turned the writ over. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> kept his eyes moving across the lot. Two cameras with clear sightlines. One blind corner behind the office shed. Three vehicles in pieces with their hoods up. At the back, in the repair corner, a young man in a work shirt had been shuffling parts around an engine block with more energy than the job called for. He'd stopped. He was standing up.

The son. Not small. Not slow. Reading the gate the way a young man reads it when he thinks his odds are better than they are.

"My own son says we should push back on this," the yard manager said. He was still holding the writ. His eyes went to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s shoulder — the sheathed sword — then to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s face. "Arpad's been a good customer. Eight years."

"Arpad bought paper that sold inside a grace window," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "That's a problem between Arpad and the co-op. Not the clinic's problem."

The son came around the engine block. He hadn't picked up a tool. Both hands empty and held wrong — too still, too deliberately open — which meant the wrench on the oil drum was the thing he was thinking about.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved without announcing it. One step right, so the gate post wasn't behind him anymore. <entity repo="motif" guid="019d6143-a8e1-7cd1-ab7c-1a4110a2ec8c">Hands</entity> open at his sides. Weight balanced. Nothing drawn. He kept his voice flat and easy.

"Your father's going to tell you to sit down. Listen to him the first time."

The yard manager looked at his son. Something passed between them in the silence — a fight they'd had before today, in a kitchen, at the end of a shift, and were having again now in the way they stood next to each other.

"Sit down," the yard manager said.

The son stopped. Two feet of distance, the wrench on the drum, and the anger with nowhere to go. His eyes went to the sword, to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hands, to his father's face.

"We should contest it?" the son asked. To his father, not to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>.

"We're going to let the man take the printer, and we're going to call Arpad and tell him he's got a co-op problem," the yard manager said. "And you're going back to that engine block until I say otherwise." He let go of the writ. "Bay three. My employee will walk you in."

The son set the wrench down on the oil drum with a sound that said everything he wasn't going to say in front of his father, went back to the engine block, and picked up a socket he didn't need.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> stayed on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hip. No rounds drawn, none spent. The son's anger was fair, and it had cost nobody anything.

The gate was open.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> had the RP-7 loaded and strapped in eleven minutes, talking to the printer the whole time in a low, even voice: "easy with the corner — that's the corner, the corner's fine — we're going to set you on a pad, not the bare deck." When the last strap was set she patted the chassis once with a wide hand, the way you'd settle a nervous horse, and climbed up front without ceremony.

The drive back to <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> Free Medical took twenty-two minutes. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> spent most of it explaining the weight-distribution tolerances of the RP-7's chassis to the printer, in the second person, as a professional courtesy.

The intake nurse took delivery on the apron at 15:40. Signed three copies. Stood a moment with her hand flat on the chassis before the bay doors rolled and it went inside.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sent <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> the confirmation at 15:43. Three words came back at 15:44: FILED AND CREDITED.

The crew logbook pinged at 15:51. He hadn't told <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> about the job.

15:40 — PRINTER RETURNED TO CLINIC. BIG WOMAN TALKED TO IT (PRINTER). PRINTER SEEMED FINE.
15:41 — THE SIGN ON THE CLINIC DOOR SAYS "NO FEE FOR CARE." DENTS ASKS: HOW?
15:44 — DENTS ALSO SAYS RAFTERS IS NOT CRYING. RAFTERS NOTES THIS IS A FACTUAL DISPUTE.
FILING SEPARATELY: BOSS DID NOT USE THE SWORD. REQUESTING EXPLANATION. — B.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pocketed the terminal and totaled the day on the apron. Writ, Φ40. Truck, Φ25. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity>'s afternoon, Φ80. That was Φ145 out against <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity>'s standard-rate fee of Φ400 — a Φ255 margin. No injury. No rounds spent. A clinic with its equipment back before the end of shift.

Then the intake nurse came back out through the bay door, and she wasn't holding a clipboard anymore. She was holding a diagnostic slate, and her face had gone the color of the apron concrete.

"It won't calibrate," she said. "The head's out of true. Whatever moved it, moved it hard." She turned the slate so he could see the fault cascade scrolling red down the screen. The print head had shifted in its carriage — not catastrophically, but enough. A millimeter, maybe. A millimeter was all it took. "We can't print on this. Not until it's re-shimmed, and we don't have the tech, and the nearest one who does is contracted to the people we took it back from." She looked at him the way you look at a man who has just handed you a debt. "It'll still print. Every line offset the same distance. Every document that comes out of this machine reads forged — timestamps, signatures, the chain of custody, all of it staged in the queue and all of it about to come out crooked. You logged it returned. <entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> logged it credited. As far as the writ's concerned, this job is closed and this printer works. It doesn't work. And now I've got a signed intake saying it does."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the three copies she'd signed. At the FILED AND CREDITED still glowing in his pocket. At the margin that had, thirty seconds ago, been clean.

The clinic's writ was official because the clinic's writ *was* official — every line true, every stamp earned. That was the whole trick of a place with NO FEE FOR CARE nailed to its door. You couldn't buy trust here, so you documented it, one honest form at a time, on a machine two payments from being owned outright. And now the machine would make every honest form look like a lie.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> came up beside him, both hands buried in her jacket pockets, and looked at the clinic door.

"Clean," she said. Thirty-two down, eight to go.

"Clean," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> agreed.

He typed back to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>: SWORD STAYS SHEATHED WHEN THE JOB DOESN'T NEED IT. THAT'S THE EXPLANATION.

She nodded once and walked toward the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> station like a woman with three more jobs before dinner who'd already arrived, in her head, at the first.

He read the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> engagement file on the walk back.

Twelve pages in <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity>'s intake format, put together by someone who understood that in the end the paper is the only argument that holds. The first eight pages were operational: scope, authorization, the tracking-dot delivery chain, the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-ed6c-7a54-97a5-56afca1f1f19">Rotterdam</entity> timestamp.

Page nine was where the sloppiness lived.

The client-reference header had carried an internal document ref through from the buyer's side — an export error, automation left uncleaned before the file went to <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity>. The header read:

REF: <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">CONTINUITY OFFICE</entity> — DISTRICT ACQUISITION PROGRAM, WEST TOWN WEST.

Below it, in the scope field, the buyer's own words: LOCATE AND MONITOR ASSET FOR PURPOSES OF ACQUISITION UNDER DISTRICT PROGRAM PROTOCOLS.

And in the authorization chain, three shells: outermost RADIAL HOLDINGS (CAYMAN), middle FORESIGHT MUNICIPAL PARTNERS, and innermost — the one that had signed the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> engagement directly — <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">CONTINUITY OFFICE</entity> ACQUISITIONS LLC, ILLINOIS.

One word appeared eleven times in twelve pages.

Not locate. Not track. Not recover.

Acquire.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped on the floor of the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> canyon. The <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> ran its low chord somewhere in the infrastructure below. He looked at the word — eleven times across twelve pages — and thought about the forged survey from the last job. SITE ASSESSED, NO ACTIVE INFRASTRUCTURE, DEAD GLASS. And the carousel junction, where the line had run warm and the room had hummed. Eight surveys, seven of them gone or edited or filed under nothing. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-60c7-75e9-8bc1-df94f90ec0b0">The Glove</entity> had spent three months building an absence into the city's record, one careful document at a time.

He reached into his coat.

Work terminal out. Screen blank.

No postings. No addenda. The standing contract still showed its last update from nine days ago. He'd reached for it three times today — on the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> landing at 08:58, at the Kessler gate while the son weighed his odds, once more on the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> apron when the nurse signed the third copy and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had half expected a note, a GRATUITY, something. Nothing. The same clean blank each time.

Whatever the client did when it read a threat had been running since morning. And it was reading the right one. Here was the hand behind the Glove — named, with shells and signatures and eleven uses of the word acquire, words that were supposed to stay buried in the metadata and hadn't.

It had known before he did. It had been watching its own address get edited out of the city's record for three months.

He put the terminal away and kept walking.

<entity repo="character" guid="019fbde4-d680-7bb7-b9f5-5f28c3b8f705">Breckenridge</entity> shook his hand at the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> door at 16:30, with the grip of a man getting back something that had been taken from him. He had his jacket on already, keys in his other hand, the ready-to-leave posture of a man who'd timed it.
